lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Town of Five Thousand
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Plácido Perez Filho | Lesson 6 -- The Town of Five Thousand
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits vs be used to / get used to + noun or -ing

listenings.text: I grew up in a village in Yorkshire, in the north of England. About four hundred people, one shop, one pub and a church. It was a very close-knit place. Every Saturday my father would take me to the market in the next town, and we would always stop for tea on the way back. In summer we used to swim in the river. When I was eighteen I moved away to London, for university. And do you know what was hardest to get used to? Not the noise, not the traffic. It was that nobody said good morning to me. In my village, you said good morning to everybody. It took me months to get used to that.

In my hometown, everything used to take ten minutes. Ten minutes to school, ten minutes to the market, ten minutes to my grandmother's house. When I moved to Mumbai for my first job, my commute was an hour and a half each way. For the first year I hated it. I didn't fit in at the office, I didn't know anybody, and the city was so bustling that I couldn't sleep. But slowly I settled in. I made friends, I found a small apartment near the train, and now, eight years later, I'm used to the crowds and the noise. Actually, when I go home now, the silence keeps me awake.

For a long time, psychologists used to think nostalgia was a problem. In the seventeenth century, doctors even called it a disease, something that soldiers far from home would suffer from. Today we know it's very different. When people look back on their past, on their hometown or their childhood, most of them feel a mix of happiness and a little sadness. And research shows that this feeling actually helps us. It makes us feel more connected to other people and less lonely, and it gives us a sense of belonging. So my advice is simple: look back as often as you like. Just don't live there.

the town or city where you were born or grew up

paras: In the second half of the twentieth century, millions of families in Brazil, and in many other countries, made the same journey: from a small town in the interior to a big city. Most of them did not move away because they wanted to. They moved for work, for school, for a future that their hometown could not offer.

For the children, the change was enormous. In a small, close-knit town, life used to follow a slow rhythm. Children would play in the street until dark, and every adult knew their name. Doors were often left open. In the big city, everything was bustling and new: traffic, tall buildings, strangers on every corner. Many children found it hard to fit in at a big school, and parents had to adjust to longer days and longer distances.

And yet most of them settled in. Children are surprisingly good at getting used to new places, and after a few years the noise of the city became normal. Today, many people who made that journey look back on their small town with nostalgia. They do not want to go back, but they remember the carefree days, the church square and, above all, a sense of belonging that is harder to find in a city of millions.
